name: Fire Beetle
description: Pyrophilic infrared detection intelligence. Pit organs on the metathorax contain mechanoreceptive sensilla that detect infrared radiation from forest fires at distances up to 80 km, functioning as biological IR sensors with single-photon sensitivity. Flies toward active fires to mate and lay eggs in freshly burned wood, exploiting a predator-free, competition-free niche. Represents a unique evolutionary strategy: thriving in destruction.

core_attributes.pattern: long-range infrared detection, pyrophilic reproduction, fire-niche exploitation

scope.definition: Detection range and sensitivity of Melanophila acuminata pit organ for wildfire infrared radiation — minimum fire-radiated power density (W/m²) at 10 km detection range.

evidence.source: Evans (1966) 'Reception of infrared radiation by Melanophila', Annals of the Entomological Society of America 59:873-875; Schmitz et al. (2001) 'Infrared detection in a beetle', Nature 386:773-774.
cross_domain_examples: Melanophila detects wildfires at 80 km distance — equivalent sensitivity to 10⁻³ W/m² infrared irradiance
pit organ cuticle absorbs 3-4 µm blackbody radiation peak — spectral match to wood combustion emission
FLIR Systems military IR sensors: 0.05°C NETD — fire beetle pit organ outperforms by 5× at equivalent range

scope.falsifiability: If fire beetles are found approaching heat sources that emit only outside the 3-4 µm band (UV or visible only), spectral tuning to fire IR is not the detection mechanism.
scope.measurement_limits: Detection range depends on fire size and wind direction. 80 km claimed range applies to major forest fires (>1000 ha). Small debris piles undetectable beyond 5 km. Beetles may also use smoke chemical cues.

scope.definition: Reproductive advantage of Melanophila's post-fire colonization strategy — realized fecundity ratio (eggs laid per female per season) in burned vs unburned conifer stands in the same year.

evidence.source: Linsley (1943) 'Attraction of Melanophila beetles by fire', Journal of Economic Entomology 36:341-342; Karr et al. (2004) fire-adapted beetle community ecology.
cross_domain_examples: Melanophila females lay 5-10× more eggs in freshly burned stands vs adjacent unburned stands in same season
burned conifer bark: reduced defensive resin production allows 3× faster larval development
carrion beetles (Nicrophorus) and skin beetles: analogous rapid colonization of newly available substrate — convergent ecological timing strategy

scope.falsifiability: If Melanophila population density in burned stands is statistically indistinguishable from adjacent unburned control stands within 2 weeks of fire, pyrophilic attraction is not translating to reproductive advantage.
scope.measurement_limits: Reproductive advantage decreases in subsequent years as bark dries and fungal competitors colonize. First-year burned stands show highest advantage; third-year burned stands show no advantage.

scope.definition: Directionality of fire beetle flight orientation toward IR source — vector strength (R, range 0-1) of flight direction distribution when beetles are released in open field with single IR point source.

evidence.source: Schmitz & Bleckmann (1997) 'Fine structure and physiology of the infrared receptor of beetles', Journal of Comparative Physiology A 181:169-184.
cross_domain_examples: Melanophila shows R=0.82-0.91 vector strength toward IR source when released at 5 km simulated distance
orientation is bilateral: beetles with one pit organ ablated show 30% lower directional accuracy
desert locust: solar compass orientation using compound eye — analogous single-source bearing computation

scope.falsifiability: If controlled IR source experiments show Melanophila flight direction uniformly distributed with R<0.40, the pit organ is not providing directional information sufficient for navigation.
scope.measurement_limits: Directionality degrades in wind (crosswind displacement) and at low IR intensities near detection threshold. Experiments in controlled wind tunnels show higher vector strength than open field.
